key_points.base: A network is a stack of simple functions: each layer multiplies inputs by weights and applies a non-
points: A network is a stack of simple functions: each layer multiplies inputs by weights and applies a non-linear activation.

Training starts with random weights, makes predictions, measures the error with a loss, then uses backpropagation, the chain rule applied layer by layer, to compute how much each weight contributed to the error.
Gradient descent nudges every weight slightly to reduce it, and this repeats over many batches.
Without the non-linearities the layers would collapse into one linear model.
Typical problems are overfitting, unstable learning rates and vanishing gradients, handled with regularization, tuning and normalization.

key_points.base: Gradient descent moves the weights against the gradient of the loss computed on all the data; SGD us
points: Gradient descent moves the weights against the gradient of the loss computed on all the data; SGD uses one example or a mini-batch, which is far cheaper per step and adds noise that can help escape poor spots.
Momentum smooths the steps.
Adam keeps running averages of the gradient and its square and gives each weight its own effective step size, so it usually converges fast with little tuning.
The learning rate matters most: too high and the loss oscillates or diverges, too low and it crawls or stalls.
I'd use a warmup and decay schedule, watch loss curves, and note that well-tuned SGD with momentum sometimes generalizes slightly better.

key_points.base: The loss encodes what counts as an error. MSE penalizes large errors quadratically, so it targets th
points: The loss encodes what counts as an error.

MSE penalizes large errors quadratically, so it targets the mean and is sensitive to outliers; MAE targets the median and is robust but has a constant gradient; Huber is quadratic for small errors and linear for large ones, a compromise.
Cross-entropy (log loss) trains classifiers to output well-behaved probabilities and is smooth, unlike accuracy, which has no usable gradient.

When errors have asymmetric business costs, such as under-forecasting being worse than over-forecasting, I'd use a quantile or custom weighted loss, and still evaluate with the metric the business uses.

key_points.base: Options in rough order of effort: get more or augmented data, simplify the architecture, add weight
points: Options in rough order of effort: get more or augmented data, simplify the architecture, add weight decay, use early stopping on validation loss, and add dropout.
Dropout randomly zeroes units during training so the network can't rely on any single path, which acts like averaging many sub-networks.
Batch normalization standardizes layer inputs within each batch, which stabilizes gradients and allows higher learning rates; it has a mild regularizing side effect but is mainly an optimization aid.
I'd first diagnose with train versus validation curves to be sure it is overfitting and not a leak or a bug.

key_points.base: I'd start with a boosted-tree baseline: on mid-sized tabular data it usually matches or beats deep m
points: I'd start with a boosted-tree baseline: on mid-sized tabular data it usually matches or beats deep models, trains in minutes, handles mixed types and missing values, and is easier to explain and monitor.
Tabular features are heterogeneous and often have sharp thresholds that trees capture well, while neural networks need careful scaling, encoding and tuning.
A network earns its place with a specific advantage: very large data, learned embeddings for high-cardinality categories, multi-task or multimodal inputs, or online updates.
I'd compare both on the same time-aware folds with comparable tuning effort, including calibration, latency and maintenance cost, and decide on the whole picture.

key_points.base: A convolutional layer slides a small filter over the input and records how strongly each location ma
points: A convolutional layer slides a small filter over the input and records how strongly each location matches a pattern, such as an edge.
Early layers detect simple patterns and deeper layers combine them into shapes and objects.
Because the same filter is reused everywhere, the network needs far fewer parameters than a fully connected one and recognizes a pattern regardless of where it appears.
Pooling summarizes regions and adds some tolerance to small shifts.
The same idea works for any grid-like data with local structure, including audio spectrograms and some time series, although for most new work a pretrained model is the starting point.

key_points.base: RNNs and LSTMs read a sequence one step at a time, passing a hidden state forward. That is inherentl
points: RNNs and LSTMs read a sequence one step at a time, passing a hidden state forward.
That is inherently sequential, so training can't be parallelized across positions, and information from early tokens has to survive many steps, which makes long-range dependencies hard.
Transformers use attention so every token can directly weigh every other token, and all positions are processed in parallel, which maps well onto GPUs and scales with data and size.
The cost is attention that grows quadratically with sequence length, which drives work on efficient variants and long-context methods.
RNN-style models are still used for streaming or very small-footprint settings.

key_points.base: For each word, the model asks a question (the query) and compares it against a label (the key) on ev
points: For each word, the model asks a question (the query) and compares it against a label (the key) on every other word; a high match means this word is relevant to me.
Those match scores are turned into weights that sum to one, and the word's new representation is a weighted blend of the other words' content (their values).
So in 'the animal didn't cross the street because it was tired', the representation of 'it' can pull in information from 'animal'.
Scores are scaled so the softmax stays well behaved, and multiple heads let the model track different relationships, such as syntax and reference, at the same time.

key_points.base: Training from scratch on 500 images would overfit, so I'd start from a model pretrained on a large d
points: Training from scratch on 500 images would overfit, so I'd start from a model pretrained on a large dataset such as ImageNet, whose early layers already detect general patterns.
First I'd freeze the backbone and train a new classification head, which is cheap and hard to overfit, then optionally unfreeze the top layers with a small learning rate.
Augmentation (crops, flips, color jitter) and early stopping help, and I'd use stratified cross-validation since a single validation split of 100 images is noisy.
If the domain is very different, such as medical scans, generic features may transfer less well, so I'd check against a baseline and consider a domain-specific pretrained model.

key_points.base: I'd start with TF-IDF and logistic regression: it trains in seconds, needs little data, is easy to d
points: I'd start with TF-IDF and logistic regression: it trains in seconds, needs little data, is easy to debug and often performs well when topics are signalled by distinctive words.
TF-IDF weights words by how specific they are to a document but has no notion of meaning, so synonyms and paraphrases look unrelated.
Embeddings from a pretrained model capture meaning and help on short or varied text, and they can feed the same simple classifier.
An LLM can classify with few or no labels, at higher cost, latency and variability.
I'd compare on one labeled test set for accuracy, cost per ticket and latency, and choose the simplest option that meets the target.

key_points.base: word2vec trains a small network on a prediction task: given a word, predict its neighbors (skip-gram
points: word2vec trains a small network on a prediction task: given a word, predict its neighbors (skip-gram), or the reverse.
The vectors that make that prediction work well end up placing words used in similar contexts near each other, following the idea that a word is defined by the company it keeps.
Limits: each word has one vector regardless of sense, so 'bank' for rivers and 'bank' for money are blended; rare words get poor vectors; and embeddings absorb biases in the training text.
Contextual embeddings from transformer models produce a different vector for each occurrence, which fixes much of the ambiguity problem.

key_points.base: Stage one is pretraining on a huge text corpus to predict the next token, which gives broad knowledg
points: Stage one is pretraining on a huge text corpus to predict the next token, which gives broad knowledge but not good behavior.
Stage two is supervised instruction tuning on examples of good responses so the model follows prompts.

Stage three, RLHF, collects human comparisons between model answers, trains a reward model to predict which is preferred, and then optimizes the chat model against that reward with reinforcement learning while keeping it close to the original.

The risk is that the reward model is only a proxy: models can learn to please raters, becoming sycophantic or verbose, which is why evaluation, diverse rater guidelines and newer preference-optimization methods matter.
